utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is Case Number IT-99-37-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Milutinovic, Dragan Ojdanic, and Nikola Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And may we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Christina Romano on behalf of the Prosecution. And here with my colleagues, Mr. Milbert Shin, Ms. Christina Miller, and Rebecca Graham.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: John Livingston for Milan Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Vladimir Petrovic. I am a lawyer from Belgrade and I'm here for Mr. Nikola Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and for Mr. Ojdanic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomislav Visnjic, lawyer from Belgrade for Dragoljub Ojdanic

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is another Status Conference, which we are having pursuant to the requirements of Rule 65. We have a number of matters to discuss. And I believe it is fair to say that the pre-trial matters are coming to some kind of a conclusion. And it is my expectation that at the end of this hearing, the pre-trial process would have been advanced significantly. First let us deal with the pending motions. We had the motion from the accused Milutinovic for provisional release. And that decision was rendered yesterday. There is a motion outstanding for protective measures. That's being considered by the Trial Chamber, and I'm in a position to say that the decision will be given shortly. There is the motion from Mr. Ojdanic for additional funds. That has been analysed by the Chamber and a decision was given which requires a response from the Registry. And the date for that response is the 13th of June. So we expect to bring that matter to conclusion shortly after the Registry puts in its response. There is the application for binding order addressed to NATO states from Mr. Ojdanic. In this regard, a further submission from Mr. Ojdanic is expected by the 20th of June. I turn now to the pre-trial brief, and I just give a brief history of the matter. At the last status conference, I instructed the Prosecution to file its pre-trial brief no later than one month after the decisions on preliminary motions were filed. The last of these decisions was issued by the Chamber on the 6th of May. And I understand that you were instructed at the 65 ter conference to have the Prosecution brief on the 6th of June. But on the 21st of May, the Prosecution filed a motion seeking a postponement of the submission of its pre-trial brief until after the Appeals Chamber had disposed of the pending appeals on jurisdiction. Two such appeals: The first one relates to the question of a joint criminal enterprise, and the decision was given on the 21st of May, 2003. But the appeal in connection with jurisdiction over events in Kosovo is still pending; however, those proceedings have been stayed by the Appeals Chamber pending the Trial Chamber's determination of the Ojdanic motion for additional funds. I have given this matter some thought. And in the circumstances, it's difficult, if not impossible, to fix a definitive date for the submission of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. So what I'm going to do is to fix a date that is related to the Appeals Chamber's ruling on the Ojdanic motion on jurisdiction over events in Kosovo, so the Prosecution will have one month after the Appeals Chamber's decision on the Ojdanic Kosovo jurisdiction matter to present its pre-trial brief. As for the Defence, the Defence will have three months after the presentation by the Prosecution of its pre-trial brief. Disclosure of witness statements, 66(A)(i) statements, disclosure completed for all three accused; 66(A)(ii) statements, disclosure again completed with the exception of nine witnesses in respect of whom an application for protective measures has been made. I made reference to that earlier and indicated that the Chamber would be ruling shortly on that issue. Expert witnesses, I understand that all expert reports have been disclosed, both in B/C/S and in English, and the only issue outstanding relates to the underlying material used for the report of the expert Patrick Ball. Here, I understand, and I will hear from the parties, that the Prosecution takes the position that it is not required to produce this material unless it forms part of the actual report. But I understand that the matter is now left for the Ojdanic Defence to inform the Prosecution of its exact concerns. So I think I'll ask the Ojdanic Defence to bring us up to date on that. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are still considering the material that we have received from the Prosecution, and we are still trying to formulate our next request. As it was said at the 65 ter conference, we already said that we would make our submission in writing. If we have any problems in this regard, we shall turn to the Trial Chamber and ask it to offer us a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's what the Trial Chamber is there for. Ultimately, if you can't resolve the matter, the Trial Chamber will resolve it on the appropriate application being made. But it is my expectation that you will be able to -- you will resolve this matter with the Prosecution. Rule 68 disclosure, this is a little bit more complicated because it is linked to Rule 70. I'll just give a very quick run-down of the history. At the last conference, I required the Prosecution to disclose to the Defence by the 10th of May all Rule 68 material for which the consent of a Rule 70 provider is required. And the Prosecution was to report to the Trial Chamber by the 10th of June whether there remained Rule 68 material for which such consent had not yet been obtained. Now, at the 65 ter conference, I understand the Prosecution confirmed that it had made all the necessary approaches to Rule 70 providers, but was awaiting responses. I just received a report from the Prosecutor on disclosure under Rule 68. So can I ask you, Ms. Romano, to comment and take us through the -- your report which I only just received.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, as it's mentioned in the report that you have received, at the Status Conference on the 13th of February, the Office of the Prosecutor indicated that 1200-person working days were necessary as you might know. We estimated to do that work within two to three months at that time. What happened after was that -- after the Prosecution deliberately and voluntarily changed the search criteria, we identified new search terms. And that is the criteria right now that you have in hands. And that copy is the most -- contains the most updated estimates for our Rule 68 search. So if you have your copy, and I don't know if the Defence has copies already? Yes, they have. If you -- I can walk you through that document. Your Honour, in the right-hand column is -- are the days remaining to be completed, the days of work remaining to be completed. If I get one search for you, and I will try to explain. For instance, if you have the name Zeljko Raznatovic, it's the fifth name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: It says that the search is in progress. So the Rule 68 search is still in progress. What happens is that when the search is done under that name, as a name, it comes up with around 2.000 documents. That's what you have. So those are the documents that are remaining to be verified. The entire range of documents that contain that name, so a search needs to be done to see if it contains Rule 68 material or not. And that work will take 27 days to be done if it is done by one person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. So that in respect of the example you have given, you have identified the number of documents, but the search has not yet been done.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The search for Rule 68 material is still in progress. And that's what -- the work will take 27 days by one person. So it goes -- at the end, you have the total estimate, that is 945 working days, a person working days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 945. Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: It's on the second page. It's at the end. This is the total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And currently our unit has approximately 25 to 30 persons, but they work in all cases of the Tribunal. So if they are to work at full-time for this search, it will take approximately two to -- excuse me. It will take approximately seven to eight weeks to be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Ms. Romano, where you have Rule 70, complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I will take you to that column. In the column that says "status," all the ones that have been done is everything has been completed, all sorts of searches, the general Rule 68 search and Rule 70 search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Including consent?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No just search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just the search.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The disclosure is why we need the consent. This is just the search of the material that we have in our possession. The ones that we have only Rule 70 complete is just the Rule 70 search has been done. We still have to do the search for the general Rule 68. Only the material -- for instance, if I go to the first Rule 70 complete is the MUP, M-U-P, the search was done only on the materials that are under Rule 70. So we have 9.400 materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the 945, which is the total, relates both to --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, those are the remaining. Those are the ones that are not under Rule 70 material. The Rule 70 search is done already, is included in the report that I gave, in the chart that we gave to you. I understand, Your Honour, it's a little bit complicated. If you have the name -- I'll try to explain again. We have under the name "MUP," we run -- what was done to comply with that line under Rule 70, we run a search under all documents under Rule 70 that contain the word "MUP" and that search has been done and the material that has been identified, a letter has been sent, and we are waiting for the provider, or maybe some of them have already been disclosed if the leave was granted. But it is the remaining documents, it's a remaining area of documents that are not under Rule 70 and that contain the word "MUP," and that work still needs to be done, and that's the one that's contained in the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Are you finished on that subject?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes. Only, Your Honour, if it's too difficult to understand, I can still run other examples, and then may be it will be clear. It took me also quite a while to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's not a matter on which I necessarily need to hear from the Defence at this stage. But if any of the counsel would like to make a comment, then you can do so now. Yes, Mr. Livingston.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: May I just ask this: Ms. Romano says that it will take, I think something like two months to complete searching all these documents. That seems to be on the basis that the full complement in the Prosecution teamwork on it. Realistically, I wonder if we could be told how many people are going to work on it and therefore realistically how long it's all going to take because it's plainly a matter, as I'm sure Your Honour will appreciate, that affects the preparation of this case and securing a fair trial for these defendants based on all the information that may assist them, because that is the whole point of the Rule 68 procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Livingston. Ms. Romano, are you in a position to say how many people are at your disposal to work on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. At the moment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Sorry. No, Your Honour. At this present moment, I can't speak for the entire office. What we know is currently we have 25 to 30 people in unit, and I have to wait to see what is the load of work. I know that in total, we will take, if using the entire unit, will take seven to eight weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the entire unit is not at your disposal, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, it's not at our disposal unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I hear what Mr. Livingston has said, but I think we have to be practical. At the same time, we have to be sensitive to the importance of this exercise for pre-trial preparation. I am satisfied that the Prosecutor is making a good-faith effort in this regard. And what I am going to do is to say that the Prosecutor must make her best efforts to complete disclosure by the time of the presentation of the -- of its pre-trial brief. That is one month after the Appeals Chamber's decision on the Kosovo jurisdiction matter. It's an ongoing exercise; and if necessary, we'll have to review it again in the light of all the circumstances. The next issue I turn to is the reciprocal disclosure under Rule 66(B) and 67(C) and my understanding is that the parties have been able to resolve any difficulties that are outstanding. If that is not so, then please say. On agreed and adjudicated facts, the Prosecution had opened negotiations on possible agreed facts, and agreement was reached in late March with the Ojdanic Defence on certain matters. The Prosecution, I understand, asked to receive responses from the other two Defence teams a week or so before the date of filing the pre-trial brief. This was found to be insufficient time to complete the task. But the parties have been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. encouraged to work hard and to agree where possible. I found in circumstances such as this that the best course for the Chamber to take is to set a date, so I'm going to set the 3rd of September as the date for the completion of these negotiations and for a report to the Trial Chamber. Rule 92 bis, this, of course, depends on the Prosecution witness list, and so we'll have to await that. But once that has been done, the parties are expected to make all possible use of Rule 92 bis. The length of trial and the number of witnesses, Ms. Romano, you just submitted a document. Would you like to take us through that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of your decision of the pre-trial brief to be extended, I would find more appropriate to discuss this by that time. If you want -- this is an estimate based on our submissions that were going to be filed on Friday. But maybe we still -- we still will have room to have -- the Defence to be more active in trying to discuss the issues with us. So I just -- or we, the Prosecution, believe that it will be more appropriate to discuss this at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I still think it would be useful for you to give an indication in the light of the present circumstances. We may have to vary it later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. I just would like to consider -- the Prosecution would like to consider this is definitely a preliminary estimate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it will only be preliminary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And we will depend on the Defence cooperation as to the continuation of this work. We also seek to reserve our position regarding the final numbers at the end. What we have here is an approximate total number of witnesses will be 140. The number of witnesses we disclosed the statement on the 31st of January, 2003, are 119. We have a number of additional witnesses that have been identified by the OTP, and we will be seeking leave to call them. And they are approximately 8. And we also have a number of additional witnesses in process of identifying or at least we know -- we intend to call the evidence on that matter. So we will give notice to the Defence about that in the pre-trial brief. There are approximately 12 witnesses. Then our estimate about live witnesses and Rule 92 bis witnesses are the following: Approximately 61 witnesses live and approximately 60 92 bis, and 11 will be experts. They will be experts under 94 bis. These will take us to a total of 220 hours, and will be 55 days. So we have an estimate additional time for additional witnesses, that would be 24 hours, equalling six days. So the total number of hours for the Prosecution case will be 240, and that will be 60 days. So it will be pretty much what we estimated at I believe in the first Status Conference when we said that we are intending to run this trial in three for four months. The exhibits, we have at the present moment, we have a total number of exhibits, approximately 1.700 -- between 1.700 and 1.800 exhibits. This is still very preliminary. I emphasise that the times I am talking here, they refer to the -- just for the Prosecution case. It does not include cross-examination, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. It doesn't include cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Does not include the cross-examination, and also does not include the time that it will -- the 92 bis witnesses will take depending on the Defence, if they have to come for cross-examination or not and how long will take the cross-examination, that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So 55 days should be almost doubled.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: It will depend on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand it's preliminary and provisional, but still useful. It is, of course, a little early for the Defence to be in a position to tell us about the length of their case. But I wonder if, Mr. Livingston, are you in a position to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not in a position to say anything about the length of our possible case. Can I simply say this: That Your Honour's absolutely right that I think all Defence lawyers are using their best endeavours to progress this pre-trial stage as quickly as we can. I think Your Honour should know that I have today handed Ms Romano a letter making certain factual admissions about the indictment which was what the Court has been encouraging. I have to say that they are limited, and there is further work to be done on that. And certainly from my client's point of view, I'd anticipate that further admissions will be forthcoming in due course. But we have made a start, and I hope it will be helpful to the Prosecution and focus attention on the actual issues in the case. Your Honour, may I just mention a couple of other matters. One of them is this: It seemed to me from Your Honour's opening comments that you're reasonably content with the way the pre-trial preparation has been proceeding to date. I think I should just sound one note of caution. While we're all doing our best, I think Your Honour is aware that there are a number of outstanding funding issues. And while I understand that Judges will only meddle in such sordid matters as funding with considerable reluctance, they are fundamental to the preparation of the Defence and the speed at which the Defence can respond. Your Honour has already referred to Mr. Visnjic's outstanding motion. I know from talking to Mr. Petrovic today that he also has an outstanding funding matter. And I can tell Your Honour there's no great secret about it that there's going to be one in respect of Mr. Milutinovic as well. And all these matters will affect the speed with which preparation of the Defence can be conducted. I hope Your Honour understands that. I'm not trying to be difficult or impolite with the Court, but it's a realistic fact. And all I can urge on Your Honour is that these matters be resolved as soon as is possible. And I'm sure that the Court will have all goodwill from the Defence insofar as we can to assist in resolving those matters. Your Honour, that was the second point. The third point I hope is a matter that can easily be dealt with. And that is this: We have, I think, all been served with a number of CD-ROMs relating to the Milosevic trial; in other words, they're of the Court hearings, daily Court hearings. Certainly, on my copies, all one has is basically a list of dates, and there's no indication given against those dates as to which witnesses testified on what day. It certainly would be helpful from my point of view, and may be it would assist my learned friends, if somebody, whether it's the Prosecution or whether it's the Registry, could provide us, because I imagine it must be in existence, could provide us with a list of which witnesses actually testified on which day in that trial. Certainly as far as the Kosovo part of the trial is concerned because otherwise it makes using these CD-ROMs almost impossible. Because one simply doesn't know where to look if one wants to find the testimony of a particular witness. So I'd be grateful if Your Honour could assist in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Livingston. I am gratified to hear of the admissions being made on behalf of your client, and I encourage the other accused to proceed along the same lines to the extent that they find it possible, to make the very best efforts because that will advance the pre-trial work and facilitate the trial itself. The last matter that you mentioned, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but I have the impression that it was only Mr. Livingston that answered the questions you put just now so I would like to be given an opportunity to give the position of our Defence team concerning the length of our case and the number of witnesses we intend to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. At this time, we are unable to give you a specific figure of witnesses that would testify during our case, or to give any specific length of time. However, in view of the speed of the pre-trial proceedings, and here I have in mind the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution which will be delivered by the deadline set by you, as well as other documents under Rule 65 ter, I believe that shortly after that, we would be able to give an assessment that would be of some value, both to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution. So upon examining these documents, I believe that we would be able to give you our first initial assessment of the length of our case. As far as the second question that you put to the Defence is concerned which pertains to the agreed facts and stipulations, I would like to convince the Trial Chamber that the Defence of Mr. Sainovic treats this issue very seriously and is trying to analyse both the evidence, the indictment itself, in an attempt to establish the facts that the sides could agree upon. So we are undertaking steps in this measure, and as soon as we're able to have something specific, we would inform both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to avail myself of this opportunity to point out an aspect of the pre-trial proceedings that has been observed by our Defence team. Given that we have agreed to reciprocal disclosure with the Prosecution, we have undertaken certain steps in our investigation, and we are encountering certain difficulties that have to do mostly with the cooperation with the government of Serbia and Montenegro as far as the documents and information are concerned. So far, we have exchanged several sets of documents with the Prosecution under Rule 67, which is our obligation. However, there are several requests of ours that are pending before the national committee of the government of Serbia and Montenegro. These requests pertain both to certain documents and to a certain type of information that was required by us from the relevant authorities. Right now, it is difficult for me to estimate for you the size of that problem; however, right now what is evident is that we are not receiving timely response to our requests. That, in turn, has impact on our obligations concerning reciprocal disclosure, and I'm afraid that this delay could also jeopardise some other deadlines, especially those deadlines that were set by you today concerning the pre-trial briefs. I would like to take this opportunity to inform you and other members of the Trial Chamber of this problem and to also say that in future, we might approach you to issue a binding order concerning this matter if the authorities in our country fail to respond to our requests. I received informally several replies, one of them was that overburdened with requests from the Prosecution. However our position is that there has to be equality of arms between the two parties, and in that respect, we might have to resort to all measures envisioned under the rules of procedure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. That, of course, is a matter for you to determine in the best interests of your client, whether you need to seek a binding order from the Chamber. And of course, as you said, the principle of equality of arms would be relevant. I just wanted to comment on Mr. Livingston's reference, Ms. Romano, to the CD-ROMs and the lack of complete information so that to render it intelligible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: If Your Honour give me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Senior Legal Officer. [Trial Chamber and Senior Legal Officer confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that the material is being provided by the Registry. And I further understand that it would be a simple matter for them to provide a list of witnesses so that the information becomes more intelligible. Thank you, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly the same information that I just obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Livingston also made reference to a more fundamental matter, the question of funding. We have received, I believe, one motion in relation to it. And it's being considered by the Chamber. It's an important matter. And the Chamber will deal with any motion that comes to it as quickly as possible. We appreciate the link between funding and the right of the accused to adequate representation, and we'll treat the matter very seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say, that it doesn't simply relate, what I was saying, to Mr. Visnjic's motion. As I understand it, and I'm sure Mr. Petrovic will tell me if I'm wrong, there is already an outstanding appeal relating to the Registrar's decision or a decision of the Registrar concerning a contribution towards his legal aid, for want of a better expression, relating to investigative and legal assistance matters. There's also a similar problem in the wings as far as my client is concerned. These are matters which fundamentally affect the way the Defence team is organised and how many investigators we can have, how the work is distributed, and ultimately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you say appeal, do you mean appeal in the strict sense? Or is it a review?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I think it may be that the strict term is a review, but nonetheless, it's a matter which comes before the Trial Chamber. And I believe that it certainly in respect of Mr. Petrovic's client, that was something that happened some months ago, and it remains unresolved. And what I'm concerned about is that it appears that my client may now be in a similar position, and I would be -- I would hope that months would not go by before his position is resolved as well. But it may be that Mr. Petrovic can help you further about the matter to which I'm referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not bringing up this issue before you today, nor do I believe that there is need to do that. But there is a decision of the Registry concerning the amount of the funding and the hours allotted for Prosecutors and legal aid. We asked that this decision be reviewed, and it is now pending before the Registry. So at this moment, I do not think that I need to trouble you with this. But you will also probably remember that you instructed the Registry to look into this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You say that it is pending before the Registry, the review, if I understand you correctly. You've asked for it to be reviewed by the Registry, not by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is our request dating back to last year. I think that it was submitted in July of last year. There was a decision made by the Registry, and we asked the Trial Chamber to review the decision. The Chamber directed the Registry as to what aspects of that decision need to be reviewed and what steps need to be undertaken. As I've said to you, the matter is now pending before the Registry, and the Registry's looking into it right now. So at the present moment, there is nothing regarding that that I would like to trouble you with. We did address you regarding this. You undertook certain steps, and depending on the decision made by the Registry and in accordance with the instructions issued by the Trial Chamber, we shall abide by that decision. I hope that I've clarified this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the matter is fully clarified now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't believe that there are any other issues unless any counsel wishes to raise anything. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I just would like to raise a couple of points, or clarify a couple of points. Your Honour, we're very grateful for the deadlines set today, and we would like to say that we intend to comply to all deadlines imposed by the Pre-Trial Judge as we have been doing this. In the past four months, a great amount of work has been done, and we intend to continue doing that and to comply to all your decisions and deadlines. I just would like to clarify that maybe I was not entirely clear. There are no more Rule 70 searches to be done. This has been completed. Any other outstanding searches that are contained in the chart that you have are general Rule 68, not Rule 70. And I just also would like to clarify that the search that you have in hands is the one that contains the extended search criteria, that we did it on the 13th of March, I believe, and we communicate same to the senior legal officer during the 65 ter conference, and also did the Defence. Regarding the Rule 68 disclosure, it's an ongoing process, it's a dynamic process, and we will do our best to complete with our disclosure. It's an evolving process, and as we identify new search terms in order to safeguard the interests of the accused, we are in a position that if we find new search criteria, and we believe this is internal, we will look for searches in this area. So I believe that the word "complete" is a little bit difficult to ascertain in this kind of process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for that clarification, Ms. Romano. If there's no other issue, then it is the right of the accused in a Status Conference to bring to the attention of the Chamber any matter relating to the -- relating to the trial or relating to the conditions of detention or any other such matter. So I'm going to start first with Mr. Milutinovic. And you can sit if you wish, in view of your condition, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I sit? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I don't know how many minutes you are ready to give to me. But I'm very concerned about everything what is going on here in the sense because I read the transcripts of the conference about Rule 65 ter, two conferences from the March 26th and May 12th. You know, I see in all those transcripts a huge confusion even between the all participants of that conference, that they sometimes don't understand each other. Later on, they clarify with all those figures about the Rules of the Procedure. And I am worried, what is the role of us as the accused? Are we are some sort of a puppet and have to be, let's say, quiet and to rely on the, let's say, capability of our lawyers or their negligence. I'm not referring to Mr. Livingston or anyone in the room. But I read carefully your lecture in Leiden from 1999. You rightly say that this is -- that this trial and this Tribunal is generous, and I agree completely with that. But the practice, I think, needs to improve some rules. Of course, I, as an indicted person, could not propose anything, but you can do it, and maybe it's impolite from my side to ask you for a private audience to give you some kind of suggestion which would improve a lot and speedness about the whole process. Because I got about 40 files, and I am so confused how to read them. I read them as I got it. But what after that? Because in all those 40 files, I can find maximum ten pages concerning me. Not more than that. So that's one question. The other question is who is, how to say, checking before coming to trial all those experts opinions? You know, when you publish a book or when you publish something in the expert field, there is some kind of supervision of that. We are going to waste a lot of time quarrelling here whether some of those, how to say, reports or opinion of the experts, correct or not. It's better that we have that before, not to be questioning only by Defence, which is very weak side for that, or maybe from the Prosecution. I'm referring about some documents which I got, and I see that those gentlemen missed the key points, that some of them are not completely aware about the law existing in Yugoslavia which they would like to analyse. So any, let's say, specialist outside of them would say then that on the beginning and save the time here on the trials. In connection with is the expert opinions of all the doctors. I didn't like to make -- is it possible to make a closed session in this part, about the medical reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but before you do that, let me tell you that I have been fairly liberal in allowing you to continue along those lines because the purpose of the opportunity which is given to you now is not for you to engage in discussions of matters that properly relate to the -- to the trial process itself. We're dealing here with pre-trial matters, and an opportunity is given to you to raise any matter relating to the conditions of detention or your health. But legal issues are issues which you can bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber through your counsel, who is very competent. So you should utilise that process, and don't use this process now to launch into legal discussions. But we will go into a private session to hear you about the medical reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I hear from Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SAINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing to say. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sainovic. Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED OJDANIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The only remaining matter is to set a date for the next Status Conference. It is required to be held on or before the 1st of October. And I'll set Wednesday, the 24th of September as the date for the next Status Conference. The hearing is adjourned.
